name: Azure Data Factory
oneLiner: Cloud data integration for ETL/ELT plus pipeline orchestration (incl. Managed Airflow).
whatItIs: Azure Data Factory is Azure's data-integration and orchestration service — and it genuinely wears both hats, which is why it appears under Integration and Orchestration. As integration, it moves data between 90+ sources with the Copy activity and transforms it visually with Mapping Data Flows (which run on managed Spark). As orchestration, its pipelines schedule, chain, branch and monitor activities — and it now also offers Managed Airflow for teams who want DAGs. On Azure it's the default glue that gets data from A to B and coordinates the steps in between.

inPractice.narrative: A pipeline needs to pull from on-prem SQL Server and a SaaS API each night, land the data in ADLS, transform it, and load Synapse — in a set order with retries and alerting. ADF's Copy activities ingest the sources, a Mapping Data Flow (on managed Spark) does the transforms, and the ADF pipeline orchestrates the whole sequence on a schedule. It's doing both jobs at once: the integration and the orchestration.

coreConcepts.detail: A pipeline is an ordered graph of activities (copy, data flow, notebook, stored proc, etc.) with dependencies, branching and retries — this is the orchestration layer.
The high-throughput data-movement engine with 90+ connectors (databases, SaaS, files, on-prem via a self-hosted integration runtime).
Visual, code-free transformations that ADF compiles and runs on managed Spark clusters — the ETL/transform side.
The compute that actually executes activities: Azure IR (cloud), Self-hosted IR (on-prem/VNet access), or Azure-SSIS IR (lift-and-shift SSIS packages).
Schedule, tumbling-window or event-based triggers start pipelines — the scheduling half of orchestration.
ADF can host managed Apache Airflow environments, so teams wanting code-first DAGs get them within the same service.

whenToUse: Moving data between many sources into ADLS/Synapse on Azure.
Code-free visual transforms (Mapping Data Flows) without writing Spark.
Orchestrating multi-step data pipelines with scheduling, retries and monitoring.
Reaching on-prem/VNet sources via a self-hosted integration runtime.
Lifting existing SSIS packages to the cloud (Azure-SSIS IR).
whenNotToUse: Heavy custom, code-first transformation logic engineers would rather write in Spark/Databricks.
Real-time streaming pipelines — use Event Hubs + Stream Analytics/Dataflow-style tools.
Simple single-trigger event glue — an Azure Function may be lighter.
Teams that want pure open-source Airflow control end-to-end (though Managed Airflow narrows this).

keyFacts.label: Two roles
keyFacts.value: Data integration (Copy + Data Flows) and pipeline orchestration.

keyFacts.label: Connectors
keyFacts.value: 90+ sources incl. on-prem via self-hosted IR.

keyFacts.label: Transforms
keyFacts.value: Mapping Data Flows run on managed Spark, code-free.

keyFacts.label: Orchestration
keyFacts.value: Pipelines with dependencies, triggers, retries; Managed Airflow option.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Per activity run + data-movement + Data Flow vCore-hours.

pricingShape: ADF bills by usage across a few axes: pipeline activity runs (a small charge per orchestration activity), data movement (priced by Copy throughput/DIUs), and Mapping Data Flow execution (per vCore-hour of the managed Spark cluster while it runs, plus cluster startup time). Self-hosted IR is free software but runs on your own VMs. There's no big always-on cluster, so cost tracks how much you move and transform. Data Flows are the usual cost driver — keeping clusters small and runs efficient matters most.
gotchas: Mapping Data Flows pay for Spark cluster startup on every run — batching transforms beats many tiny flows.
Self-hosted IR is your responsibility to install, patch and scale — it's a VM you own.
It plays both integration and orchestration roles; teams sometimes overload pipelines with logic better done in Spark/Databricks.
Debugging visual Data Flows over large data can be slow; test on samples first.
Event/tumbling-window triggers have semantics worth understanding to avoid missed or duplicated runs.

equivalents.name: AWS Glue
equivalents.note: Serverless Spark ETL + catalog; Step Functions/MWAA cover orchestration on AWS.

equivalents.name: Cloud Data Fusion
equivalents.note: Visual integration; Cloud Composer handles orchestration on GCP.
